C004.subject: Social media platforms with algorithmically curated feeds that prioritize close relationship content
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Social media platforms with algorithmically curated feeds that prioritize close relationship content subjective well-being than chronological feeds]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment comparing algorithmic (close-tie-prioritizing) vs. chronological feed conditions on platforms like Facebook or Instagram, measuring daily subjective well-being (e.g., PANAS, Cantril ladder) over 4-6 weeks. — Directly tests causal effect under real-world conditions, controlling for confounds like usage intensity and baseline well-being, and can verify the qualifier condition about algorithm accuracy.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on social media feed curation and well-being, focusing on effect sizes for close-tie vs. weak-tie content exposure (e.g., Burke & Kraut, 2016; Verduyn et al., 2017). — Synthesizes available evidence to assess consistency and magnitude of the hypothesized effect, identifying gaps in current research and moderators like algorithm transparency or user engagement.

[PATH:empirical] Cognitive-affective mechanism study using experience sampling to capture momentary well-being and perceived social support when users encounter algorithmically surfaced close-tie content vs. chronological posts. — Tests the theoretical pathway: whether close-tie content boosts well-being through increased belongingness or reduced social comparison, clarifying why the effect might occur and under what conditions.

scope.domain: adult users in developed countries who use social media primarily for maintaining close relationships

qualifier.condition: when the algorithm successfully identifies and surfaces content from close ties over weak ties or non-social content

C005.subject: Social media platforms
C005.object: net negative effects on subjective well-being
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Social media platforms net negative effects on subjective well-being]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel study tracking social media usage patterns and subjective well-being (e.g., SWB scales like PANAS or SWLS) over 6-12 months among adult users in developed countries, with specific focus on close-relationship maintenance behaviors. — Longitudinal data can disentangle causal direction and assess whether the hypothesized negative effects persist or attenuate over time, addressing the disputed status and condition about close relationships.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiment comparing subjective well-being outcomes between groups assigned to use social media primarily for close-relationship maintenance vs. other purposes (e.g., information seeking), with pre/post measures of social comparison, FoMO, and perceived depth of interaction. — Experimental designs can isolate the causal role of the qualifier conditions (social comparison, FoMO, superficial engagement) and directly test the proposed mechanism.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on social media use and well-being, stratified by relationship maintenance vs. other use types, and controlling for baseline well-being and demographic confounds. — Synthesizing available evidence can reveal effect size consistency, publication bias, and whether the net negative effect holds specifically under the stated condition, helping to confirm or refute the hypothesis with higher confidence.

qualifier.condition: when used for maintaining close relationships, due to increased social comparison, fear of missing out, and substitution of deep interaction with superficial engagement

C006.subject: Active social media engagement with close-tie networks
C006.object: net positive effects on subjective well-being by increasing perceived social support
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Active social media engagement with close-tie networks net positive effects on subjective well-being by increasing perceived social support]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal diary study tracking daily social media interactions with close ties and subsequent measures of perceived social support and well-being in adolescents/young adults — Captures the temporal dynamics and reciprocal communication specified in the qualifier, allowing causal inference about the effect of active engagement on well-being via perceived social support.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental manipulation where participants engage in structured emotional disclosure with close ties on a social media platform vs. passive browsing, with pre/post measures of perceived social support and well-being — Directly tests the mechanistic claim that reciprocal emotional disclosure strengthens relationships and increases perceived support, isolating the effect from passive consumption or weak-tie interactions.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies comparing effects of social media interaction with close vs. weak ties on subjective well-being, focusing on moderation by reciprocity and emotional disclosure — Synthesizes available evidence to confirm or refute the hypothesis across multiple contexts, identifying effect sizes and boundary conditions (e.g., age, platform type).

qualifier.condition: when interactions involve reciprocal communication and emotional disclosure
qualifier.mechanism: strengthening of existing relationships rather than weak-tie maintenance

C007.subject: Social media platforms
C007.object: net positive effects on subjective well-being
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Social media platforms net positive effects on subjective well-being]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel study tracking adolescent social media use patterns (active vs. passive) and self-reported well-being over 2-3 years, controlling for baseline mental health and offline social support. — Directly tests the causal claim under the specified qualifier (active use for relationship maintenance) and scope (adolescents/young adults), addressing the disputed status with time-lagged data.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies on social media interventions designed to foster community building (e.g., private group chats, shared interest forums) and their effects on subjective well-being measures. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether active, community-oriented use consistently yields net positive effects, clarifying the disputed hypothesis across multiple contexts.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework integrating socioemotional selectivity theory and uses-and-gratifications approach to predict differential well-being outcomes based on active vs. passive social media engagement. — Provides a mechanistic explanation for why active relationship maintenance might produce net positive effects, guiding empirical tests and refining the hypothesis's conditions.

qualifier.condition: when used actively for relationship maintenance and community building
